thread.title: Why T. Rowe Price Likes Alphabet, Amazon, and Facebook

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Why T. Rowe Price Likes Alphabet, Amazon, and Facebook

organizations.name: t. rowe price science and technology

text:
Photo: Gabriella Demczuk By Tiernan Ray April 13, 2018 9:00 a.m. ET Ken Allen isn’t one to let the market tell him he’s wrong about a company. The manager of the T. Rowe Price Science and Technology fund (ticker: PRSCX) looks for what the market has missed when it unloads shares of a company generating lots of cash. That’s what he did with Facebook amid its recent travails. Allen, 40, believes that a handful of innovators, including not just Facebook, but also Amazon.com and Alphabet , have tremendous “runway,” as he terms it, or gigantic market opportunities they’re uniquely equipped to exploit. He recently shared some of his ideas with Barron’s .
Barron’s : What’s your thesis in owning some of the biggest tech names?
Allen: The biggest reason I own a lot of Amazon [AMZN], Facebook [FB], and Alphabet [GOOGL] is that the share those companies have in their addressable markets is still really low, despite their having been incredible businesses for a long time. Amazon’s share of the tech market it’s addressing [with cloud computing services] is less than 5%. And e-commerce as a portion of total retail globally is somewhere in the low double digits, so it has less than 5% share of the total global retail market excluding China, where Alibaba obviously dominates. Amazon has these two huge opportunities where it has less than 5%. Facebook is around 5% of the total global advertising market excluding China. Google is in the low double digits of total advertising share. Given the positions of those three companies, their user bases, and all their vast capabilities, it makes sense that their market shares will all be dramatically higher at some point. I don’t worry about a shortening runway for the three, despite their being epically successful already.
The market in February and March became extremely concerned about trade wars and also about increased regulation for the giants. How did you handle that?
One of the things I look for most in tech stocks is to buy great growth businesses that are on sale. There is an opportunity to create a lot of alpha for tech investors because the industry is so dynamic, and there are periods when there are dislocations. I see particular opportunity in Facebook following the selloff, based on my confidence the company will continue to grow at attractive rates. In some cases, expectations for future earnings and cash flow come down and a stock comes down. In this case, though, our expectations haven’t meaningfully changed [as far as cash flow] and the stock is down 15%. My contention isn’t that Facebook is somehow risk-free, but I’m comfortable with the various risks, which have been well-discussed.
What about the worry that there are many other shoes to drop about how Facebook could be regulated?
It’s incumbent on them to effectively navigate what has become a tougher environment from a data-privacy and prospective regulatory standpoint. I believe the company is positioned to do so for several reasons, including its technology capabilities, its data, its massive network of users—over two billion monthly active users at this point—and its top talent, the people who are able to leverage all those capabilities to figure this out and get it right.
‘ “I see particular opportunity in Facebook following the selloff, based on my confidence the company will continue to grow at attractive rates.” ’
It seems there are some reasons for encouragement, based on the company’s actions in recent months. For instance, making account settings and privacy settings clearer and easier to adjust, based on just one’s own interest in certain mechanics of their Facebook presence. When advertisers were surveyed or interviewed, the feedback is relatively encouraging. The overwhelming number of advertisers are unlikely to spend less on or pull spending from Facebook, in particular.
Illustration: None The other thing that is important to my investment in Facebook is that we have an extremely high regard for Instagram, which is much less in the crosshairs of these regulatory issues. It’s an incredibly vibrant, high-usage social network. I’m of the view that they’ve been fairly conservative so far with ad load [volume of ads]. There’s a lot of opportunity still to come. I don’t have some kind of algorithm in mind for how quickly and at what ultimate level it can be monetized. I think there’s the opportunity for advertisers to create more engaging ads than on other platforms because of the nature of Instagram. If advertisers are smart and creative, with Instagram’s help, a dramatically higher ad load than exists probably wouldn’t become a problem for users, either.
How about Amazon?
Amazon I have liked for a really long time. It’s obviously had an enormous run. But when I start to think a lot about the very high medium-term valuation multiples, what I always keep in mind is that, ultimately—I don’t know if it’s five or 10 years from now—Amazon will have the biggest market cap of all companies. I also think Alphabet and Microsoft [MSFT] are attractive here, and based on our positioning in those two, I hope they make it hard for Amazon to get to that market cap! But, ultimately, I think the combination of the size of Amazon’s market opportunity—bigger than probably any company in the world—and the company’s position to unlock those opportunities, will make it the biggest market cap in theworld. We try to make extra sure we have confidence in the longer term and have really good reasons to think a company won’t get disrupted, that it will be the disrupter. Amazon is in that category of great innovators that will disrupt in more and more areas for years to come.
How about the valuation?
I do worry that the stock is expensive on any sort of medium- to near-term multiples, but ultimately I care most about the lifetime cash flows. I think Amazon is going to have margins longer-term, as its investments pay off, that are even higher than what is reflected in the stock. People still think about Amazon margins as being like retail margins. But within that, they have this big marketplace business where margins are much higher [collecting fees on sales by third-party merchants]. Given the scale of Amazon’s retail business, there are benefits in terms of volume purchases from suppliers, pricing power, and developing more and more of its own brands over time, which can be high-margin. AWS [Amazon Web Services cloud computing], which is already a great tech business and is going to be one of the biggest tech businesses anywhere, we already see doing well over 20% operating margins. That’s a leading indicator of the kind of free-cash-flow margins it can ultimately generate, which can be much higher than retail. Its advertising business isn’t going to be bigger than Google’s is now, and is unlikely to be as big as Facebook’s is now for a couple of decades, but it will probably be the highest-margin of the three businesses for them. All that basically gets to my view that for the very long term, free-cash-flow margins can be somewhere in the double-digit range.
Newsletter Sign-up And as for Alphabet?
Alphabet is starting to give reason to ascribe some value to its nonadvertising businesses. With Waymo [Google’s self-driving subsidiary], the large investments Google has been making for many years in that business are getting fairly close to providing some kind of payoff in terms of getting cars on the road, or more cars on more roads, and eventually building a business model around it. Needless to say, the auto market and the transportation market are enormous. I think there’s a good likelihood Google will be able to make Waymo a valuable enough business that it is impactful to Google’s stock price. And while Google’s cloud computing business is no AWS or Azure, long-term it has a strong enough position and sufficiently differentiated capabilities to become another fairly valuable payer in the overall cloud-technology market.
Anything that’s too rich that you would avoid?
There will be great growth businesses I just don’t own because I don’t think they’re at great prices. The one that stands out is Netflix [NFLX]. I think Netflix has a very good chance of continuing to thrive and becoming a dramatically bigger business, and not being disrupted by Amazon or Google, or others. I put Tesla [TSLA] in that category as well. Both have strong prospects, and both are burning cash, but in Tesla’s case, I own a lot of it, and in Netflix’s case, I don’t own any of it. What’s different is that from a longer-term cash flow perspective, I think Tesla will generate more than enough cash to make the stock well worth owning, at this price. If Tesla can execute as we think they can with the ramp of the Model 3—there are a lot of risks to that—they’ll be generating meaningful cash flow before Netflix is able to generate meaningful cash flow. Positive cash flow for Tesla later this year is in the range of outcomes I consider, but my investment isn’t predicated on that.
You have been very critical of Apple in the past as one stock you won’t own among large-cap tech. Still feel that way?
Among the big seven tech names, including two in China, Alibaba Group Holding [BABA] and Tencent Holdings [0700.Hong Kong], which I do own, I favor several of them over Apple [AAPL] because I think they have longer growth runways than Apple does. That gets to the market-share numbers that I was mentioning for Google, Amazon, and Facebook. Apple’s obviously an extraordinary company, and they execute well and are investing a lot in innovation, and they built a much larger services business than they had historically. That’s all positive. I just think it’ll be more challenging to deliver enough growth than it will be for some of the others.
Are you worried the trade-war talk could lead to a disruption in the electronics-supply chain?
Broadly speaking, tech stocks seem to be embedding more potential of an adverse scenario for their businesses around prospective tariffs. Where I see particular opportunity is when great growth businesses are particularly on sale.
What about the prospects of recession? You’ve managed money here entirely within the period of a massive recovery from recession, so you’ve not yet dealt with that.
It’s one of the most important questions. It’s been an incredible historic run [for the market] since the lows of early 2009, especially for tech. I started managing in early 2009, and that was obviously lucky timing! Basically, the fund returned almost 500% since that point. While T. Rowe as a firm had really good performance prior to the long bull market, and at least as good during the long bull market, I think that we will probably do at least as good a job in a tougher market. Because we are really rigorous about what a truly good business is, and rigorous about valuation. I think we have the ability to avoid more of the big losers, while still owning the ones that will be winners. If we’re right about that, buying them when they are down because of recession or a bear market can be a really good opportunity.
Thanks, Ken.
